title: Bhringi and the half-woman god
hookLine: a sage tries to worship Shiva without the goddess, and Shiva becomes half her
carry: shiva and shakti are never apart
tomorrow: tantra has a reputation. what does a Tantra say about it?
last: FROM THE GATES TO THE DOT.

cards: There's a story told in many temples about a sage named Bhringi, who loved Shiva so fiercely he would honor no one else. Not even the goddess.
When he came to Mount Kailasa to walk his circle of honor, he meant to circle Shiva alone. Parvati, seated beside Shiva, moved closer, so there was no way between them.
So Bhringi, the tellings say, became a bee and drilled through the narrow gap. What does Shiva do with a devotee like that?

teach.b: In one common telling, Parvati takes back what every body gets from its mother, the flesh and blood, and Bhringi is left too frail to stand, until Shiva, gently, gives him a third leg to lean on. Then Shiva settles it.
He takes Parvati into himself and stands as Ardhanarishvara, the lord who is half woman: one side Shiva, one side the goddess, one body. Now there's no gap to fly through.
That image stands in temples across India, and it carries the teaching: Shiva and Shakti are never apart.
Shakti means power, and in tantric thought it's also the goddess's own name, because she is that power. Two schools honor the pair from different sides.
Shaktas, who worship the goddess as the highest, quote the first verse of the Saundarya Lahari: joined with Shakti, Shiva can create; without her, he can't so much as stir.
Shaivas, who worship Shiva as the highest, say he is pure awareness, the ground, and Shakti is his power, the way heat belongs to fire. They differ on which name to say first.
What neither does is what Bhringi did. You can love one side more. You can't worship one by cutting out the other.

how: Shakta Hindus worship the goddess as Shakti, the divine power itself, in hymns like the Saundarya Lahari and in worship at home and in temples.

games.q: what does “what tantra actually is” mean?
o: two rival gods who compete for the same worshippers
Shiva and Shakti: awareness and power, never apart
a god and his wife, who rules only while he's away

games.q: two voices, one pair. tap the pairs.
p: power, and the goddess's own name
the lord who is half woman

s: Shiva and Shakti are two rival gods competing for worship
neither school calls them rivals; both say the two are never apart.
in Bhringi's story, Shiva answers by becoming half the goddess
Ardhanarishvara: one body, so no one can honor one and skip the other.
Shakti means power, and is also the goddess's name
in tantric thought she is that power.

games.q: a Shaiva friend says Shiva is the ground and Shakti is his power. you're asked to give the best case for the Shakta side. what do you say?
o: without her, the verse says, he can't even stir: everything that moves is her.
the goddess appears in more stories than Shiva, so she must outrank him.
Shiva is only awareness, and awareness isn't really anything at all.
games.why: the Shakta case rests on the power that moves everything; the Shaiva case on the ground beneath it. both say the two are never apart, as Ardhanarishvara shows.

practice: If you pray, say the two names together, softly, Shiva, Shakti, one pair on each out-breath.

If you don't, sit with your back steady, still as a hill, and let the breath move however it likes: the stillness that holds you up and the motion that never stops, together. For this sit, don't choose between them.

wordCard.voice: What tantra actually is: here, Shiva and Shakti, awareness and power, never apart, like Ardhanarishvara, half Shiva, half the goddess.

orig.note: Sanskrit: power, energy; in tantric thought, also the goddess's own name.

carryVoice: Keep this one: Shiva and Shakti are never apart. Not even a bee fits between them. Day sixteen-thirteen, done.

sources.ref: The story of Bhringi and Ardhanarishvara (Bhringi circles Shiva alone, as a bee; loses the strength of his body and is given a third leg; Shiva unites with Parvati as Ardhanarishvara). Tellings differ; told in Shaiva temple traditions and Puranic retellings
Saundarya Lahari, verse 1 (Shiva, when united with Shakti, is able to create; otherwise he is not able even to stir)
Shaiva and Shakta tantric teaching on Shiva as awareness and Shakti as power, inseparable
